Augmented methanogenic performance in straw-manure co-digestion via 
micro/nano bubble-enhanced syntrophic metabolism
Yanning Hou a, Chao Liu a, Jianhong Wei b, Wenyan Zhao a,*
, Binghua Yan a
a College of Environment & Ecology, Hunan Agricultural University, Changsha, Hunan 410128, PR China
b College of Bioscience and Biotechnology, Hunan Agricultural University, Changsha, Hunan 410128, PR China
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C  A B S T R A C T
• NBW treatment yielded the highest 
methane production over other aeration 
methods.
• Enzyme activities and microbial di­
versity 
were 
enhanced 
in 
NBW 
treatment.
• Less energy was spent to cope with the 
ROS oxidation stress in the NBW 
treatment.
• Methanosaeta (91.66 %) were key 
archaea for methane production.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Methane production
Micro/nano-bubble
Swine manure
Rice straw
Anaerobic co-digestion
A B S T R A C T
This study aimed to investigate the enhancement of methane production by comparing air-nanobubble water 
(air-NBW) and conventional micro-bubble aeration during the anaerobic co-digestion (AcoD) of rice straw and 
pig manure. Remarkably, the addition of air-NBW (T3-NBW), as the most effective gas supplementation strategy, 
resulted in the highest cumulative methane yield of 489.49 mL/g⋅VS with a minimal lag phase of 0.57 days, 
representing a 59.80 % increase over the control (306.49 mL/g⋅VS, p < 0.001). This finding aligns with the 
kinetic fitting data (477.85 ± 5.84 mL/g⋅VS), wherein the maximum methane production rate for the T3-NBW 
was 41.89 mL/g•VS⋅d−1. Mechanistic insights revealed that air-NBW dramatically elevated the activity of 
β-glucosidase (hydrolysis) and coenzyme F420 (methanogenesis) by 82.72% and 133.8 %, respectively, compared 
to the control. These results suggested that the efficient conversion of intermediate products played a critical role 
in enhancing overall methane yield. Microbial community analysis identified acetotrophic methanogenesis as the 
dominant pathway, with Methanosaeta abundance reaching 91.66 % in NBW-amended treatments. Additionally, 
the co-occurrence network analysis showed that the air-NBW system promoted microbial interaction and sta­
bilized the ecological network. Crucially, the NBW treatment exhibited the lowest expression of energy- 
dependent antioxidant enzyme genes (e.g., superoxide reductase, SOR), suggesting reduced oxidative stress 
and enhanced energy allocation toward microbial growth and methanogenic activity. By enhancing oxygen

1. Introduction
As global energy shortages and environmental pollution issues 
intensify, the demand for sustainable and renewable resources is expe­
riencing rapid growth (Khan et al., 2021). Biomass, like rice straw and 
pig manure, is recognized as a renewable energy source. The annual 
production of rice straw and pig manure are approximately 900 million 
tons and 700 million tons in China, respectively (Chang et al., 2021; 
Wang et al., 2022). However, most of these waste streams are not 
effectively treated and utilized, which leads to biomass resource loss but 
also pollutes the environment (Im et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2017). Biogas 
production from anaerobic digestion (AD) provides a promising 
approach to mitigating environmental pollution but also alleviating 
energy shortages (Li et al., 2024).
Recently, anaerobic co-digestion (AcoD) has been widely used to 
enhance biogas production from biomass. Generally, rice straw features 
in high carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio and rich lignocellulosic content 
while pig manures are characterized by a lower C/N ratio. Direct 
anaerobic fermentation of these individual substrates often leads to 
excessive accumulation of organic acids or ammonium, resulting in the 
failure of the anaerobic system. The AcoD of rice straw and pig manure 
provides a better macro- and micro-nutrient balance, pH buffering ca­
pacity, and process efficiency (Wang et al., 2018). Nevertheless, recal­
citrant lignocellulosic structure limits the hydrolysis and mass transfer 
rate during the co-digestion of straw and pig manure, which remains a 
great challenge for methane production. Strategies like biochar addition 
and thermal pretreatment were found to be able to facilitate this prog­
ress (Chuenchart et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Moreover, micro-aeration 
technology, introducing air-microbubbles (MBs, with diameters of 
1–100 μm) or nanobubbles (NBs, with diameters of <1 μm) into the 
fermentation liquid, has recently emerged as an effective way to 
enhance the performance of the AD process (Zhou et al., 2022). It was 
reported that limited oxygen content can increase microbial diversity 
and promote the enrichment of facultative hydrolytic bacteria, thus 
accelerating the biodegradation of organic matter (Ding et al., 2024).
Nanobubble water (NBW) has attracted significant attention in the 
AD process due to its unique properties, including long-term stability, 
negative surface charge, and the ability to generate reactive oxygen 
species (ROS) (Hou et al., 2024). The NBs can be maintained in water for 
extended periods because they are almost unaffected by buoyancy in 
solution. Previous studies have shown that the bubble (~140 nm) in air- 
NBW remained for 14 days, maintaining a stable micro-oxygen envi­
ronment over the long term, thereby enhancing methane production 
(Wang et al., 2019). In addition, NBs show a high microbial adhesion 
due to the characteristics of negative surface charge and high zeta po­
tential (Hou et al., 2024). The large specific surface could ensure suffi­
cient contact between microorganisms and substrates, further 
accelerating the biochemical reaction. Research has demonstrated that 
NBW accelerated the consumption of volatile fatty acids (VFAs), 
avoiding their accumulation and associated inhibitory effects, thereby 
strengthening the syntrophic metabolism (Fan et al., 2024). Moreover, 
air-NBW was reported to be able to significantly enhance electron 
transfer under high salinity conditions, leading to a 21–65 % increase in 
hydrogen yield and a 14–43 % increase in methane yield (Hou et al., 
2021a). Furthermore, NBs have been proven to generate ROS: when 
nanobubbles collapse, the rapid release of internal pressure generates 
substantial surface energy, facilitating the conversion of oxygen mole­
cules into ROS, including hydroxyl radicals (•OH), superoxide anions 
(O2
•−), and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) (Hou et al., 2024). On one hand, 
ROS was considered to be beneficial for facilitating the degradation of 
complex organic compounds. For instance, •OH possesses robust 
oxidizing properties that can readily cleave C–O and C–C bonds in 
lignin, leading to lignin depolymerization (Guengerich & Yoshimoto, 
2018). This accelerates cellulose degradation and increases soluble 
organic matter content, thus resulting in an elevated cumulative H2 
yield (Zhu et al., 2023b). However, some studies indicated that excessive 
ROS can disrupt membrane integrity, impair metabolic pathways, and 
ultimately compromise the overall efficiency of the digestion process 
(Liu et al., 2016b).
Traditional microbubble aeration has been demonstrated as an 
effective strategy to enhance the process efficiency during the AD pro­
cess (Fu et al., 2022). Microbubbles usually dissolve and collapse more 
rapidly, resulting in lower gas transfer efficiency and an increased 
propensity for gas leakage during aeration. This not only complicates the 
AD process but also poses a potential explosion risk (Chuenchart et al., 
2021). In contrast, NBs distinctly improve gas dispersion and gas–liquid 
mass transfer, while simultaneously reducing energy consumption 
(Zhou et al., 2022). Moreover, there are still some controversies on the 
ability of ROS generation of MBs/NBs. Some studies suggested that MBs 
are more prone to rupture, leading to larger amounts of ROS generation 
than NBs (Ohgaki et al., 2010). However, some researchers insisted that 
NBs were more conducive to the production of •OH. The amount of 
exogenous •OH has a positive relationship with the NB number density 
in the water (Liu et al., 2016a). Therefore, a systematic comparative 
study on the impact of MBs/NBs on AcoD performance and the microbial 
response is needed.
In this study, microbubble-aeration and air-nanobubble water were 
proposed to enhance the performance of the AcoD of rice straw and pig 
manure. The impact of different aeration strategies on the hydrolysis- 
acidification process and methanogenesis was discussed. Furthermore, 
a comprehensive investigation of the microbial community structure, 
co-occurrence networks, key enzyme activities, and functional gene 
expression related to antioxidant defense systems based on the Kyoto 
Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database was performed to 
reveal the possible metabolic pathway and underlying mechanism. 
These findings are expected to provide new insight into more efficient 
methane production from biomass and contribute to the development of 
the circular economy.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrates and inoculum
Rice straw and pig manure were used as substrates in this study. Rice 
straw and pig manure were collected from the experimental field and the 
livestock and poultry breeding center of Hunan Agricultural University, 
respectively. Before the experiment, the rice straw was first cut into 
small pieces and then sieved through a 20-mesh sieve. After removing 
undigested feed, hair, and large impurities, the collected pig manure was 
thoroughly mixed. The inoculum used in the experiment was anaerobic 
granular sludge purchased from Qingdao Liboyuan Environmental 
Protection Materials Co., Ltd. (Shandong). The sludge was pre-cultured 
in a thermostatic chamber at 37 ± 1 ◦C for one week. The main

2.2. Preparation and characterization of microbubble aeration and NBW
The air-NBW used in this experiment was prepared by North China 
Electric Power University (Nanolf1500 series, Shanghai Xingheng 
Technology Co., Ltd.). The concentration and size distribution of the NBs 
were analyzed and measured using a nanoparticle tracking analyzer 
(NS300, Malvern). The Zeta potential was measured using a Zeta po­
tential analyzer (Zetasizer Nano ZS90). MBs are generated through a gas 
diffuser connected to a micron-sized aeration head, driven by a peri­
staltic pump (LongerPump BT100-2J) with a head capacity of Longer 
YZ1515x.
2.3. Experimental setup
Serum bottles with a total volume of 500 mL were used as the AD 
reactor. The substrates were a mixture of pig manure and rice straw with 
a wet weight ratio of 2:1. The initial TS concentration was set at 6.7 %. 
Four treatments were set: control (T1-DW), air microbubble-aeration 
(T2-MA), air-NBW (T3-NBW), and the combination of air-NBW and 
air-microbubble-aeration (T4-NBW-MA). In this experiment, 320 mL of 
deionized water was added to the T1-DW and T2-MA treatments, while 
320 mL of air-NBW was added to the T3-NBW and T4-NBW-MA treat­
ments. The fermentation experiment lasted for 29 days. Samples were 
collected every day in the first 9 days and afterwards, samples were 
taken every two days. After each sampling, the T1-DW and T2-MA 
treatments were supplemented with an equal volume of deionized 
water, while the T3-NBW and T4-NBW-MA treatments were supple­
mented with an equal volume of air-NBW. Additionally, to maintain the 
presence of microbubbles, 150 mL of ambient air was continuously 
injected into the T2-MA and T4-NBW-MA treatments at a flow rate of 
0.83 mL/min after each sampling. All the tests were carried out in 
triplicate.
2.4. Analysis methods
2.4.1. General parameters
The C/N ratio contents were determined using an elemental analyzer 
(German element Elementar, MACRO cube). Total solids (TS) and vol­
atile solids (VS) were measured according to standard methods. Soluble 
carbohydrate concentration was measured by using the Phenol-sulfuric 
method. Soluble protein concentration was determined with the Coo­
massie Brilliant Blue method. The volume of biogas produced during the 
experiment was measured using a medical syringe method. The 
composition of the biogas (CH4, CO2, H2) was analyzed using a gas 
chromatograph (LC-20A, Shimadzu, Japan). The digested samples were 
centrifuged, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 µm mem­
brane for VFA analysis using high-performance liquid chromatography 
(DJS-1C, LeiMagnet, Shanghai, China); meanwhile, chemical oxygen 
demand (COD) was determined by the potassium dichromate method. 
The activities of β-glucosidase and coenzyme F420 were measured using 
UV spectrophotometry. The collected samples were centrifuged, and the 
pellets were used for microbial community analysis by Novogene Co., 
Ltd. The co-occurrence network analysis was performed using R-Project 
(version 4.4.2), and the resulting network was visualized using Gephi. 
The relative abundances of bacteria and archaea were determined via 
16S rRNA sequencing. The functional gene expression related to the 
dominated metabolic pathway and antioxidant defense was analyzed 
using the KEGG database.
2.4.2. Kinetic models
The modified Gompertz model was used to study the methane pro­
duction process. This model was employed to calculate the maximum 
methane production potential, the maximum methane production rate, 
and the lag phase. The model is shown in Eq. (1).

2.4.3. Statistical analysis
Origin 2018 was employed for plotting all data in this study. Single- 
factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted using SPSS version 
26.0 to test the significance of differences, with a significance level 
assumed at p ≤0.05.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Properties of air-nanobubble water
Air-NBW was generated by introducing air into deionized water 
using a nanobubble generator. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a–b), the air-NBW 
exhibited a narrower size distribution of 50–300 nm compared to the 
deionized water (50–500 nm). The size distribution of air-NBW in this 
study was a little different from the previous research on air-NBWs 
(144–223 nm) (Wang & Yang, 2019). The slight variations in bubble 
distribution can be attributed to disparities in nanobubble generation 
equipment and process-specific conditions, such as gas injection pa­
rameters and water quality. Furthermore, the size distribution curve of 
the air-NBW remained nearly constant (from 15:21:15 to 15:26:09) 
while the bubble size distribution of ordinary deionized water showed a 
significant variation over the monitoring period (from 14:40:23 to 
14:44:58). This indicates that air-NBW exhibited greater stability over 
time compared with the deionized water.
The zeta potential of the prepared air-NBW and deionized water was 
also measured (Fig. 1c). Air-NBW exhibited a significantly more nega­
tive zeta potential (-18.7 mV) than deionized water (-7.14 mV). The zeta 
potential value was close to the reported value (-20 mV ~ -17 mV) 
measured in the water after the introduction of NBs (Ushikubo et al., 
2010). This high negative zeta potential was attributed to the adsorption 
of hydroxide ions on the NB interface, forming an electrical double layer 
of ions and counter ions (Chuenchart et al., 2021). The increased ab­
solute value of the zeta potential implied stronger interfacial charge 
density and enhanced electrostatic repulsion, contributing to higher 
colloidal stability. In summary, air-NBW had prolonged the gas–liquid 
interfacial behavior within the system, thereby creating a more favor­
able microenvironment for gas transfer, enabling sustained oxygen 
supply, and promoting substrate degradation and microbial metabolism, 
which was consistent with the findings in Section 3.3.
Air-NBW demonstrated distinct physicochemical properties, char­
acterized by a bubble size distribution ranging from 50 to 300 nm, the 
negatively charged, and elevated zeta potential in comparison to 
deionized water. These features increased specific surface area and 
enhanced substrate–microbe interactions, accelerating biochemical re­
actions during AD. Previous research has shown that NBs improved gas 
transfer and ozone dissolution in viscous systems (Hu & Xia, 2018). In 
addition, NB collapse generated ROS, including •OH radicals, which 
facilitated substrate degradation but could be harmful to microbes if 
overly abundant (Liu et al., 2016b). Overall, it was expected to optimize 
the AD process by stimulating microbial metabolic activity with air- 
NBW supplementation.
3.2. Effect of micro/nanobubbles aeration on methane production
The cumulative and daily methane production profiles under 
different strategies were illustrated in Fig. 2. It was found that the

3

treatments (T2-MA, T3-NBW, T4-NBW-MA) exhibited significantly 
higher cumulative methane production (351.94–489.49 mL/g⋅VS) 
compared to the control (T1-DW, 306.49 mL/g⋅VS) (Fig. 2a). This 
indicated that micro-aeration strategies significantly promoted the 
performance of methanogenesis during AD. Among these, the T3-NBW 
treatment demonstrated the highest cumulative methane yield of 
489.49 mL/g⋅VS, representing a 59.80 % enhancement over the control. 
The T4-NBW-MA and T2-MA treatments achieved cumulative methane 
productions of 408.74 mL/g⋅VS and 351.94 mL/g⋅VS, corresponding to 
33.36 % and 14.83 % increases compared to the control, respectively. 
The highest methane yield observed in this study was significantly 
higher (67.67 %) than that reported value (291.77 mL/g⋅VS) in other 
studies involving the co-digestion of straw and pig manure (Han & Ning, 
2024). The significant enhancement in methane production observed in 
this study was attributed to the addition of air-NBW which enhanced the 
degradation efficiency of organic matter and stimulated microbial ac­
tivity. Furthermore, variations in substrate composition and operational 
conditions likely alleviated the accumulation of VFAs, thereby opti­
mizing the micro-environment. The daily methane production profile 
(Fig. 2b) revealed that massive methane production occurred during 
days 1–15 for all treatments, coinciding with the decomposition of 
macromolecular into VFAs. Minor methane was produced afterward. 
Notably, the T3-NBW treatment reached peak daily methane production 
(70.59 mL/g⋅VS⋅d−1) on day 5, demonstrating an improvement of 
108.96 % over the control (33.78 mL/g⋅VS⋅d−1). This enhancement 
observed during the start-up period may be attributed to the effect of 
NBs on the accelerated breakdown of complex organics, thereby rapidly 
releasing bioavailable VFAs (Chuenchart et al., 2021). Notably, the cu­
mulative methane production of T3-NBW treatment reached 310.37 
mL/g⋅VS during days 2–9, accounting for 63.4 % of the total methane 
production. These results demonstrated that the T3-NBW treatment 
outperformed other aeration methods (microbubble aeration and the 
combination of microbubble-nanobubble aeration) in the methane 
production from the AcoD of pig manure and straws. In summary, the 
addition of NBW enhanced methane production in the AD of rice straw 
and pig manure without causing secondary pollution.
In this study, the kinetic behavior of methane production during the 
anaerobic co-digestion of pig manure and straw was systematically 
evaluated using the modified Gompertz model (Fig. 2c–f). Notably, the 
T3-NBW treatment exhibited superior methanogenic performance, 
achieving a maximum cumulative methane production of 477.85 ±
5.84 mL/g⋅VS, which represented a 58.45 % enhancement compared to 
the control (301.56 ± 3.24 mL/g⋅VS). This result closely aligns with the 
actual methane yield measured in this study (489.49 mL/g⋅VS), 
demonstrating that the model accurately described the variation in cu­
mulative methane production (R2 > 0.9846). Previous research reported 
a predicted maximum cumulative methane production of 335.25 mL/ 
g⋅VS by the Gompertz model under similar experimental conditions 
(initial TS content of ~6 %) (Tian & Gong, 2023), which was obviously 
lower than the value observed in this study. Building on this once again 
demonstrated the superiority of air-NBW in enhancing methane pro­
duction during co-digestion. Furthermore, the kinetic analysis revealed 
two critical advantages of NBW supplementation: (1) NBW enhanced the 
methane production rate: the maximum methane production rate for the 
T3-NBW treatment reached 41.89 ± 2.03 mL/g⋅VS⋅d−1, a 50.90 % in­
crease over the control (27.76 ± 1.23 mL/g⋅VS⋅d−1); (2) NBW shortened 
the microbial adaptation phase: the lag time (λ) of T3-NBW treatment 
was significantly reduced to 0.57 days, indicating the improved eco­
nomic efficiency of the anaerobic system.
3.3. Impact of micro/nanobubbles aeration on hydrolysis/acidification
The hydrolysis process involves the conversion of complex organic 
compounds (such as polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids) into smaller 
soluble molecules, which is recognized as the rate-limiting step for 
methane production. As shown in Fig. 3(a), the soluble polysaccharide 
profile decreased until day 9 due to microbial uptake, surged from days 
9–13 via enhanced hydrolysis, and finally declined as methanogenesis

dominated. This V-shaped trajectory conformed to the typical batch 
operation. On day 13, the polysaccharide concentration in the T3-NBW 
treatment (346.68 mg/L) had increased by 13.14–24.64 % compared 
with the other three treatments. (278.14–305.80 mg/L). This phenom­
enon was also in agreement with the previous work (Zhu & Lyu, 2023a). 
In addition, the soluble protein concentration followed a comparable 
trend of first increasing and decreasing across all four treatments 
(Fig. 3b). The highest soluble protein concentration was reached at day 
9. Compared with the control, the soluble protein concentration in the 
T2-MA, T3-NBW, and T4-NBW-MA treatments increased by 8.07 %, 
34.12 %, and 10.92 %, respectively. Furthermore, the high specific 
surface area and sufficient interfacial area of NB increased opportunities 
for contact with microorganisms, thereby promoting rapid interaction 
and utilization of soluble polysaccharides and soluble proteins, and ul­
timately accelerating their release (Hou et al., 2024). This might explain 
the enhanced release of soluble polysaccharides and soluble proteins in 
the T3-NBW treatment. The results showed that the highest concentra­
tions of soluble protein and polysaccharides in the T3-NBW treatment 
highlight its superior efficacy in hydrolyzing complex substrates. 
Additionally, the T3-NBW treatment exhibited the highest COD con­
centration, indicating the facilitated soluble organic matter released 
from the straw and manure. Moreover, the COD concentration in the T3- 
NBW treatment increased at a significantly faster rate than in other 
treatments from day 4 to day 17, reaching a peak on day 17 that was 
21.91 % to 35.85 % higher than the others (Supplementary Material). 
The superior performance of the NBW treatment during the hydrolysis 
stage was likely attributed to the smaller size and higher stability of 
nanobubbles, which enabled sustained oxygen release and localized 
charge formation (as shown in the results of Section 3.1). Overall, these 
results indicated that the T3-NBW treatment significantly enhanced the 
solubilization of organic matter, further supporting its effectiveness in 
promoting substrate hydrolysis.
Macromolecular organic compounds are further decomposed into 
VFAs during AD, which are key intermediates for methane production. 
As depicted in Fig. 3(c–f), acetic and butyric acid emerged as the pre­
dominant metabolites, accompanied by relatively minor concentrations 
of valeric acid, propionic acid, and formic acid. Acetotrophic meth­
anogenesis was identified as the dominant pathway. Among these, a

small amount of propionic acid existing in all treatments was conducive 
to the stability of the digestion system. During the first 4 days, acetic 
acid was the main product while butyric acid became the predominant 
product afterward. Butyric acid can be converted into acetic acid or 
other intermediate products, further promoting methane production 
(Wang et al., 2021). The concentrations of total VFAs (including valeric 
acid, butyric acid, propionic acid, acetic acid, and formic acid) remained 
low (<645.59 mg/L) during the early and late stages of AD in all 
treatments. The consistently low concentration of VFAs in the anaerobic 
reactor strongly indicated efficient methanogenic performance. VFAs 
accumulation (556.10–2136.09 mg/L) mainly occurred during 5–9 d, 
which was due to the hydrolysis of the complex substrate. Interestingly, 
it was clear that the control (T1-DW) showed relatively higher total 
VFAs than other treatments (T2-MA, T3-NBW, and T4-MA-NBW). This 
suggested that the micro-aeration strategies promoted the syntrophic 
relationship between the acidogens with methanogens, thereby 
improving the utilization of VFAs in time.
The production of butyric acid and acetic acid (BA + AA) in each 
treatment was present in Fig. 3(c–f). In the first 2 days, the total con­
centration of BA + AA in the T2-MA, T3-NBW, and T4-MA-NBW treat­
ments ranged from 72.98 % to 85.27 %, which was slightly higher than 
that in the control (T1-DW). This indicated that the micro-oxygen con­
ditions in these treatments promoted the generation of butyric and 
acetic acid. Notably, on day 9, the combined concentration of BA + AA 
in the T3-NBW treatment reached 95.13 mg/L, which was significantly 
higher than the 40.91 mg/L observed in the control. The elevated con­
centration of butyric and acetic acid implied the availability of sub­
strates during the methanogenesis phase, which could subsequently 
support the growth and metabolism of methanogen. The result indicated 
that the addition of NBW significantly improved the degradation of 
organic matter and enhanced the release of soluble compounds, which 
subsequently enhanced methane production.

The dynamic variation of the microbial diversity under distinct 
micro-aeration strategies was also investigated (Supplementary Mate­
rial). Notably, T3-NBW consistently exhibited the highest Chao1 and 
Shannon indices, indicating enhanced species richness and diversity. For 
example, on day 27, the Chao1 index in the T3-NBW treatment was

(659.77–745.66). This increased biodiversity contributed to greater 
system stability and correlated positively with methane yield (Fig. 2). It 
was inferred that the larger specific surface area of the NB enhanced the 
contact area between the bubbles and microorganisms, thereby 
improving the performance of AD. Prior studies also suggested that NBs 
facilitate microbial attachment through stronger electrostatic in­
teractions (Hou et al., 2024). The microbial community structure of 
bacteria and archaea at the genus level in the four treatments was pre­
sented in Fig. 4(a–b). The dominant bacterial genera were Psychrobacter,

and

The Christensenellaceae_R-7_group was related to acetic and butyric

was consistent with the higher concentrations of acetic and butyric acids 
in these treatments, indicating a dose-dependent relationship between 
gas input and the relative abundance of Christensenellaceae_R-7_group, 
which can promote VFAs production. On day 9, Psychrobacter—a pre­
dominantly aerobic or facultatively anaerobic genus adapted to low 
temperatures (Bakermans, 2018)—transiently dominated in T2-MA 
(61.46 %) and T4-NBW-MA (44.99 %), likely due to air/oxygen sup­
plementation that promoted the degradation of complex substrates (e.g., 
proteins, lipids) into acetate and isovalerate, thereby supporting syn­
trophic interactions with methanogens in the AD system. As fermenta­
tion progressed, unidentified_Synergistaceae became increasingly 
dominant in all treatments during the later stages (days 17, 27, and 29). 
Their relative abundances ranged from 19.15 % to 52.31 %. This 
dominance was likely due to their ability to degrade proteins and car­
bohydrates into acetate and isovalerate. They can also supply electrons 
for methane production when easily degradable substrates are limited 
(Tomazetto et al., 2018), thereby contributing to their ecological 
advantage at this stage. Additionally, in the T3-NBW treatment, the 
abundances of DMER64 and Ruminofilibacter increased by 9.45 % and 
3.81–7.97 %, respectively, compared to the control. DMER64 may 
enhance the degradation of disaccharides (Zhuang et al., 2021), while 
Ruminofilibacter can promote the degradation of cellulose and hemicel­
lulose (Tan et al., 2025). These increases in abundance suggested that 
NBW, with its high surface area and stability, had facilitated microbial 
attachment and enhanced the hydrolysis of complex carbohydrates.
Methanosaeta and Methanobacterium are key participants in methane 
production during AD. Methanobacterium, a methane-producing bacte­
rium with some tolerance to oxygen (Fu et al., 2016), showed relative 
abundances of 34.98–61.19 % during days 2–9 across all treatments. 
Among these, T4-NBW-MA (61.19 %) and T2-MA (54.39 %) treatments 
exhibited increases of 31.89 % and 17.06 %, respectively, compared to 
the control. This enhancement was likely due to elevated gas levels in 
the T2-MA and T4-NBW-MA treatments, which facilitated Meth­
anobacterium growth. Methanosaeta is a strict acetoclastic methanogen 
that produces methane from acetate and releases carbon dioxide as a 
byproduct, playing a key role in AD (Ma et al., 2021). In this study, 
Methanosaeta dominated in all treatments on days 17, 27, and 29, with 
relative abundances ranging from 37.29 % to 91.66 %. Given the limited 
acetate content in the VFAs, it was inferred that Methanosaeta utilized 
acetate as a substrate for acetotrophic methanogenesis. Notably, T3- 
NBW significantly enriched Methanosaeta, achieving a relative abun­
dance of 91.66 %. This indicated that the addition of NBW promoted the 
growth of Methanosaeta, thereby enhancing the acetoclastic methano­
genesis process.
Co-occurrence network analysis was employed to investigate the 
correlations among the top 40 dominant bacterial genera across four 
treatments, aiming to elucidate the potential interactions between mi­
croorganisms (Fig. 4(c–f)). The network relationships of the four treat­
ments had 97 (T1-DW), 97 (T2-MA), 151 (T3-NBW), and 109 (T4-NBW- 
MA) edges, respectively. Notably, the network of the T3-NBW treatment 
was more complex. Additionally, the proportion of positive interactions 
and symbiotic relationships in T3-NBW (58.28 %) was higher than that 
in the other three treatments. The addition of NBW enhanced microbial 
interactions and stabilized the ecological network in AD by promoting 
more intimate cooperation among microbes.
Unidentified_Synergistaceae emerged as one of the dominant bacterial 
genera in the T3-NBW treatment, significantly accelerating the hydro­
lysis and acidification of complex organic matter. This genus exhibited 
positive co-occurrence with 5 microorganisms, including Methanosaeta 
and DMER64. Methanosaeta is an acetoclastic methanogen that utilizes 
acetate to produce methane (Hong et al., 2024). The positive correlation 
between Methanosaeta and Unidentified_Synergistaceae suggested that 
NBW had enhanced the effective utilization of acetate by improving the 
solubility of organic matter and optimizing mass transfer processes, 
thereby promoting microbial synergy. Notably, Psychrobacter demon­
strated a positive co-existence with 9 distinct microbial species in the 
T3-NBW treatment. In contrast, only 1–2 similar co-existence relation­
ships were observed in the other treatments (T1-DW, T2-MA, T4-NBW- 
MA). Given the high specific surface area of NBW, the rupture of NBs 
could enhance the diffusion of substrates and metabolic products. This 
process enabled Psychrobacter to share substrates or metabolic in­
termediates with a wider array of microorganisms, thereby further 
strengthening interactions within microbial communities. For instance, 
the co-occurrence between Psychrobacter and Acinetobacter (a genus 
known for degrading aromatic compounds) may be attributed to the 
promotion of hydrophobic substrate dispersion by nanobubbles. Addi­
tionally, NBW can effectively alleviate oxidative stress, promoting the 
coexistence and cooperative metabolism between strict anaerobes and 
facultative anaerobes.
3.5. Functional enzymes and the proposed metabolic pathway
3.5.1. Key functional enzymes
β-glucosidase and Coenzyme F420 are two key enzymes involved in 
methane production from AD of biomass, respectively. Among them, 
β-glucosidase plays a pivotal role in the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic 
biomass, specifically in the conversion of cellulose disaccharides into 
glucose (Park et al., 2015). Compared to the control treatment, the ac­
tivity of β-glucosidase in three treatments (T2-MA, T3-NBW, T4-NBW- 
MA) was enhanced to varying degrees (Supplementary Material). 
Notably, the T3-NBW treatment exhibited the highest increment of 
β-glucosidase activity over other treatments: 44.14 %, 64.94 %, 82.72 
%, and 67.02 % on days 2, 9, 17, and 27, respectively. The enhanced 
enzyme activity could result in an improved hydrolysis process. This 
result also coincided with the highest methane production in T3-NBW 
treatment. Moreover, protease activity under NBW treatment 
remained consistently higher than that of the control throughout the 
digestion process, with a peak of 698.24 U/mL in the mid-stage—55.37 
% higher than the control (449.41 U/mL). This significant enhancement 
further demonstrated the positive role of NBW in facilitating the hy­
drolysis process. Coenzyme F420, a specific enzyme that plays a crucial 
role in methanogenesis, can serve as an indicator of methanogen activity 
within AD processes (Hou et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2019). The T3-NBW 
treatment significantly increased coenzyme F420 activity by 53.17 %– 
133.80 % compared to the control. On day 13, the activity of coenzyme 
F420 in the T3-NBW treatment reached 28.10 U/mL, representing a 
133.77 % increase compared to the control. This was consistent with 
previous findings that NBW addition enhanced coenzyme F420 activity in 
straw AD (Cui et al., 2024). On one hand, NBs possess high surface 
charge characteristics, which can enhance the catalytic efficiency of 
hydrolytic enzymes through adsorption-mediated mass transfer effects. 
On the other hand, their large specific surface area and hydrophobicity 
provide additional attachment sites for microorganisms, facilitating 
metabolic processes, accelerating organic matter degradation, and ulti­
mately improving methane production (Niu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 
2019). Thus, the addition of air-NBW enhanced the activity of key en­
zymes in the hydrolysis and methanogenesis stages of straw, thereby 
further boosting methane production.
3.5.2. Proposed metabolic pathways
Based on the metabolic functions from the KEGG database, the 
metabolic pathway for methane production during AD after the addition 
of air-NBW was proposed (Fig. 5c). Initially, during the hydrolysis 
phase, complex organic molecules (e.g., cellulose and glucose) are 
degraded by microorganisms into simpler compounds, such as mono­
saccharides. In the T3-NBW treatment, the activity of endoglucanases

(EC 3.2.1.4) was 117.31 % higher than that in the control, indicating 
that the introduction of NBW significantly enhanced cellulose degra­
dation through the hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds, thereby promoting 
the production of glucose and facilitating subsequent acid fermentation 
(Fu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2023a). The hydrolyzed monosaccharides are 
converted into pyruvate via the glycolytic pathway, with 6-phosphofruc­
tokinase (EC 2.7.1.11) playing a crucial role in converting glucose to 
pyruvate, generating ATP and NADH in the process. Notably, the ac­
tivity of 6-phosphofructokinase in the T3-NBW treatment was 54.81 % 
higher than in the control, enhancing sugar metabolism and energy 
production. Subsequently, under low oxygen conditions, pyruvate is 
decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, 
entering the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, where it undergoes further 
oxidation to CO2 and water, releasing energy and producing NADH and 
FADH2 (Chen et al., 2020). The activity of α-ketoglutarate dehydroge­
nase complex (EC 2.3.1.61, 1.2.7.11, 1.2.7.3), a key enzyme in the TCA 
cycle, was also elevated in the NBW treatment. The enhanced surface 
charge and zeta potential of NBW facilitated microbial adsorption and 
aggregation, which in turn promoted the accumulation of intermediate 
products during both acidogenesis and methanogenesis stages. In the 
methanogenic phase, Methyl-coenzyme M (EC 2.8.4.1) reductase ac­
tivity in the T3-NBW treatment was 202.06 % higher than in the control, 
contributing to the increased methane yield by catalyzing the final step 
of methane production from methyl-CoM. These results indicated that 
the addition of NBW enhanced methane production by upregulating the 
metabolic functional genes involved in the hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and 
methanogenesis stages of AD.

2023), activating the antioxidant defense system (such as superoxide

research investigated the expression of antioxidant enzymes under 
different treatments based on the KEGG database (Fig. 5a). The results 
showed that the expression of energy-independent antioxidant enzyme- 
related genes (kat, gpx, SOD1, SOD2, ginA, nifH, KatG) in the T3-NBW 
treatment was significantly lower than in the other three treatments. 
This indicated that NBs could effectively maintain appropriate ROS 
levels and ensure system stability, but these enzymes typically generated 
oxygen as a byproduct. In contrast, the T4-NBW-MA treatment exhibited 
the highest expression of antioxidant enzymes, reflecting that the com­
bination of NBW and micro-aeration intensified ROS generation, 
prompting microorganisms to upregulate detoxification mechanisms 
(Liu et al., 2016a). Notably, energy-dependent enzymes such as SOR in 
methanogens can also eliminate ROS without producing oxygen (Wu 
et al., 2021), and coenzyme F420 can act as an electron donor to drive 
ROS scavenging reactions (converting ROS into harmless molecules, 
such as water instead of oxygen) (Martins et al., 2019). The T3-NBW 
treatment not only showed lower SOR abundance but also exhibited 
the highest coenzyme F420 enzyme activity. It is estimated that coen­
zyme F420 in T3-NBW treatment may participate in ROS elimination by 
energy-dependent enzymes like SOR. In conclusion, the T3-NBW treat­
ment exhibited the lowest antioxidant enzyme expression, conserving 
energy for microbial growth and further metabolic activity. Moreover, 
future studies should incorporate advanced in situ detection techniques 
such as Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) spectroscopy to elucidate the 
dynamic generation and transformation mechanisms of reactive oxygen 
species.
4. Conclusions
This study demonstrated that T3-NBW treatment outperforms other 
aeration methods in enhancing methane yield during the AcoD of rice 
straw and pig manure. The results showed that the addition of NBW 
achieved the highest methane yield (489.49 mL/g⋅VS), representing a 
59.80 % increase compared to the control. In addition, NBW signifi­
cantly enhanced the activities of key enzymes (hydrolytic and meth­
anogenic enzymes) and promoted a metabolic pathway dominated by 
acetotrophic methanogenesis. Further analysis revealed that NBW 
facilitated the development of positive microbial interactions and sym­
biotic relationships. Moreover, the presence of NBW reduced the energy 
consumption required by energy-dependent antioxidant enzymes to 
cope with ROS stress, thereby contributing to improved methane pro­
duction. As a green and environmentally friendly additive, NBW offered 
advantages such as simple operation and low cost. It effectively allevi­
ated the hydrolysis limitations in the AcoD system of rice straw and pig 
manure, significantly improving organic matter conversion efficiency 
and energy output.
